paras: The attempted lynching of Miller and Clarke was a failed attempt by a mob on the night of Tuesday, July 17, 1888, to take two white men held on rape charges from the jail in Knoxville, Tennessee, and lynch them. Officers at the jail stopped the attempt, and five men, among them a newspaper editor and a reporter, were arrested as members of the mob.

According to the Asheville Citizen, Knoxville had "two rape cases on hand this week, both by white men on two little white girls." One of the accused, Clarke, was charged with assaulting Frances Robinson, a 12-year-old white girl and the daughter of a washerwoman, near the city limits on the evening of Tuesday, July 17. A Knoxville dispatch named him as William Carter, alias Clark, and said he was arrested at his home about 1 a.m., identified by a Black man who had seen him walking with the girl and then by the girl herself, and jailed. No details of the case against Miller appear in the coverage.

On Tuesday night a crowd tried to take both men from the jail, but in the Asheville paper's words "the determined action of the officers at the jail prevented mischief." A Kentucky news summary reported that two attempts to lynch Clarke had failed. Two days later, a Knoxville wire said the excitement continued, with hundreds of people on the streets and near the jail, which was under a strong guard.

Five persons were arrested, charged with being implicated in the mob, including C. W. Crozier, editor of Opinion, and W. D. Peters, a reporter. No report of their hearings, or of the trials of Miller and Clarke, was found.

The episode reached distant papers as brief items. The Washington Critic ran the wire as "Concerned in a Lynching" and called the prisoners "the rapists" as fact, and the Camden Evening Telegram printed the same text a day later under "Excitement Over an Attempted Lynching." In redating the wire to July 20, the Camden paper changed "Tuesday night" to "night before last" in its first sentence while keeping "Tuesday night's mob" in a later one. The Stanford, Kentucky, Interior Journal called Clarke "a fiend," while the Emporia Weekly News, which reprinted the July 18 dispatch under "A Little Girl Brutally Assaulted," called the accused "the villian" and "the demon" and noted only "considerable talk of lynching." Several reports stressed that the accused and the girls were white, and none commented on the mob beyond the arrests.

The reports disagree on timing. The wire and the Asheville item placed the attempt on Tuesday night, but the July 18 dispatch has Clark arrested early on July 18 and jailed after an identification that afternoon, which would put any attempt on him after Tuesday night.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Miller and Clarke
bases: A crowd tried to take two jailed men accused of rape and lynch them, and officers at the jail stopped it (A1, A2, A3).

The papers report an attempted lynching of two men accused of rape that officers prevented; no one is reported killed (A1, A2, A3). Five men were arrested as part of the mob, so a group of three or more acted outside the law (A1).
The Knoxville wire (A1) and the Asheville Citizen's separate local item (A2) agree that a Tuesday night attempt to lynch the jailed men failed, and A3 reports two failed attempts.

framing.detail: Headlined 'Concerned in a Lynching' and called the jailed men 'the rapists' as fact, while reporting the arrests of the mob suspects without comment.
Asheville's item said 'the feeling of indignation is very high' and credited the officers' 'determined action' with preventing 'mischief'.
The Kentucky summary called Clarke 'a fiend' and noted the failed lynching attempts without comment on them.
The Emporia reprint, 'A Little Girl Brutally Assaulted', dwelt on the assault, calling the accused 'the villian' and 'the demon', and mentioned only 'talk of lynching'.

Miller and Clarke (Clark); one dispatch names Clark as William Carter, alias Clark.
Both accused of rape of young white girls; Clarke's accuser named as Frances Robinson, 12.
A mob; five men arrested as implicated, including editor C. W. Crozier and reporter W. D. Peters.
Tuesday night, July 17, per the wire and Asheville; a July 18 dispatch's timeline puts Clark's jailing after that night, so the date is uncertain for the attempt on him.
Attempts at the jail to seize the prisoners (a siege of the jail); no pursuit is reported.
